title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injury
case: Case: A 19-year-old footballer felt a pop while landing and fell. The knee swelled within 2 hours. He cannot fully straighten it. Lachman shows more forward movement than the other knee with a soft end-point. Valgus stress is normal. Pulses and sensation are normal. He wants to return to football.

Working diagnosis: suspected ACL tear. Plan: exclude fracture through a doctor, control swelling, restore full extension and quadriceps activation, MRI and orthopaedic opinion, discuss reconstruction versus rehabilitation in view of his sport, begin criteria-based rehabilitation.

differentials.name: Meniscal tear
differentials.key: Joint-line pain, locking, catching, delayed swelling

differentials.name: PCL injury
differentials.key: Fall onto the front of the shin, posterior sag

differentials.name: Tibial plateau or other fracture
differentials.key: Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness

differentials.name: Knee dislocation (multiligament)
differentials.key: Gross instability, possible vessel and nerve injury

qa: Why is the Lachman test preferred over the anterior drawer? It is usually more sensitive and easier to perform in a painful, guarded knee [Ref - to verify].
Why check pulses and sensation? A knee dislocation or severe ligament injury can damage vessels and nerves, which is an emergency.
Why is regaining full extension so important early? Loss of extension can cause lasting walking and strength problems and makes later recovery harder [Ref - to verify].
Why not rely on a fixed number of months for return to sport? Strength, control and confidence vary between people. Returning too early is linked to re-injury, so criteria matter [Ref - to verify].
The patient has an unstable knee that keeps giving way despite good rehabilitation. What next? Discuss reconstruction with the surgeon because repeated giving way risks further injury to the knee.

fields.Purpose: Check for increased forward movement of the tibia on the femur
fields.Patient position: Supine, leg relaxed, knee bent about 20 to 30 degrees
fields.Therapist position: Beside the knee being tested; one hand stabilises the lower thigh, the other holds the upper shin behind the tibial head
fields.Action: With the thigh held still, pull the tibia forward in a smooth, firm movement. Feel the amount of movement and the quality of the end-point. Repeat on the other knee
fields.Positive: More forward movement than the uninjured knee, with a soft or absent end-point
fields.Negative: Similar movement to the other knee, with a firm end-point
fields.Limits: A negative result does not fully exclude a tear, especially in acute injury with guarding or a large effusion, or with some partial tears [Ref - to verify]. Large hands or a large thigh can make the test hard
fields.Common errors: Knee bent too far; the thigh not stabilised; hamstring contraction; the foot not relaxed
fields.Next step: If positive, check associated injuries and arrange medical review and imaging

fields.Position: Supine, hip bent to 45 degrees, knee bent to 90 degrees, foot flat on the bed
fields.Action: Sit lightly on the foot to hold it, hold the upper shin with both hands, and pull the tibia forward
fields.Positive: Increased forward movement compared with the other knee
fields.Limits: Less sensitive than the Lachman test, especially in acute injury, because hamstring guarding and swelling limit it [Ref - to verify]

fields.Purpose: Reproduce the rotational instability of an ACL-deficient knee
fields.Position: Supine, leg relaxed, hip slightly flexed
fields.Action: Hold the foot and shin, apply an inward rotation to the shin and a valgus stress while moving the knee from extension into flexion
fields.Positive: A sudden shift or clunk as the tibia reduces, usually at about 20 to 40 degrees of flexion
fields.Limits: Very specific when positive, but hard to perform in an awake, guarded patient; not often possible in the acute stage [Ref - to verify]

fields.Positive: Increased opening compared with the other knee; pain
Backward shift or sag of the tibia

redFlags.Finding: Gross instability in several directions, severe swelling, history of a high-energy injury
redFlags.Why it matters: Multiligament injury or knee dislocation, possibly with vessel injury
redFlags.Immediate action: Check foot pulses and colour; call emergency services if abnormal

redFlags.Finding: Foot drop or numbness over the outer lower leg and top of foot
Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness, deformity
Hot red knee with fever after injury or surgery

manual.name: Patellar mobilization
manual.why: Prevent stiffness, support extension and flexion
manual.finding: Reduced patellar glide after injury or surgery

manual.name: Gentle tibiofemoral mobilization for stiffness
manual.finding: Persistent loss of extension or flexion

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: early active rehabilitation. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not use techniques that force anterior tibial translation. Avoid aggressive stretching into a swollen knee.

exercise.Exercises: Heel slides, passive extension holds, quadriceps sets, straight leg raise, walking with aids as needed, ankle pumps
exercise.Objective: Reduce swelling, regain full extension and flexion, activate the quadriceps
exercise.Progress when: Minimal swelling, full extension, good quadriceps control

exercise.Exercises: Sit-to-stand, mini-squats, leg press, step-ups, hip and calf strengthening, stationary bike
exercise.Progress when: Pain and swelling stay low; strength improving

exercise.Exercises: Single-leg balance, single-leg squats, deceleration drills, walk-to-run progression
exercise.Progress when: No swelling after loading, good control, adequate strength

exercise.Exercises: Cutting, jumping, change-of-direction drills, sport drills

exerciseNotes: Principle: progress by criteria, not by weeks. Early goals are controlling swelling, regaining full extension and quadriceps activation. Later goals are strength, landing control, running readiness and sport-specific work [Ref - to verify].
Quadriceps strengthening: closed-chain and open-chain knee extension are both used, and loads and ranges are adjusted to avoid pain and strain on the graft after surgery [Ref - to verify].

Return to sport criteria (example): near-normal strength (often 90 percent or more of the other leg), hop test performance of 90 percent or more of the other leg, no swelling or giving way, good movement quality, and psychological readiness assessed with a tool such as the ACL-RSI. Many programs delay return to pivoting sport until about 9 months or longer after reconstruction, because returning earlier has been linked with higher re-injury risk [Ref - to verify]. No fixed date is set here.
Injury prevention: neuromuscular training (strength, landing technique, balance) reduces ACL injury risk in sport [Ref - to verify].

modalities.name: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation for quadriceps
modalities.indicated: Possible when voluntary quadriceps activation is poor
modalities.comment: May help early activation [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: After surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol for bracing, weight-bearing and range limits.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Mechanism, rapid swelling and a positive Lachman or pivot shift? Yes: working diagnosis is suspected ACL tear. Refer for imaging and orthopaedic opinion, and begin early rehabilitation.

Decide with the patient and surgeon between rehabilitation first and reconstruction. Factors that favour early surgery include a young athlete returning to pivoting sports, repeated giving way, a repairable meniscal tear or multiligament injury [Ref - to verify].
A rehabilitation-first approach is reasonable for many patients, including those with lower demands, with surgery later if instability continues [Ref - to verify].
Acute: screen flags and the neurovascular status, protect the knee, control swelling, restore extension and quadriceps activation.
Decision: discuss rehabilitation first or reconstruction with the patient and the surgeon.
Rehabilitation: progress by criteria through strength, landing control, running and sport drills.
Return to sport: assess by objective and psychological criteria, not by time alone.
